'''''Aquilegia canadensis''''', the '''Canadian columbine''', '''Canada columbine''', '''eastern red columbine''', or '''wild columbine''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[buttercup family]]. It is a [[perennial plant]] that is native to the woodlands and rocky areas in eastern North America in both the United States and southern Canada. It readily [[Hybrid (biology)#Hybrid plants|hybridizes]] with other plants in the [[Aquilegia|columbine]] genus and is a common garden plant.

==Description==
Canadian columbine is an herbaceous perennial growing {{Convert|15|–|90|cm|in|0|sp=us}} tall in the wild,{{sfn|Whittemore|2020}} occasionally reaching as much as {{Cvt|1|m|ft}}.{{sfn|Sutherland|1986|p=89}} It produces its stems and leaves from a substantial [[caudex]],{{sfn|Sutherland|1986|p=89}} a vertically oriented underground stem.{{sfn|Wennerberg|2006|p=1}} Its roots are short-lived and fibrous.{{sfn|Wennerberg|2006|p=1}} The hollow stems are often entirely hairless, but can have very fine, short, and erect glandular hairs on the upper parts or covering the whole stem.{{sfn|Sutherland|1986|p=89}}

The leaves are two times [[ternately]] compound, each leaf divided into three parts with three leaflets, nine in total, though older sources report that they can have three ternate leaves.{{sfn|Whittemore|2020}} Leaves attached to the stems are smaller than the [[basal leaves]], those springing directly from the caudex.{{sfn|Bare|1979|p=116}} Basal leaves are much shorter than the flowering stems, reaching lengths of {{Cvt|7|to(-)|30|cm|round=0.5}},{{sfn|Whittemore|2020}} though more typically {{Cvt|10|to(-)|20|cm}} including the main [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]].{{sfn|Bare|1979|p=116}}

The leaflets of Canadian columbine are broadly ovate, egg shaped in outline, to almost round, but with wavy teeth or lobes.{{sfn|Gleason|Cronquist|1991|p=60}} The surface of the leafletes are always hairless, but the underside can be covered in very fine and short hairs giving a pale appearance.{{sfn|Nold|2003|p=72}} The leaves are green to blue-green, and remains evergreen at temperatures down to {{cvt|-10|°F|°C|order=flip}} and as high as  {{cvt|110|°F|°C|order=flip}}. At these extremes the plant goes dormant and sprouts new leaves when favorable conditions return.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}}

Canadian columbines start blooming in spring, as early as March in their native habitat,{{sfn|Whittemore|2020}} or as late as July in early summer.{{sfn|Bare|1979|p=116}} Flowering continues for about one month, dependent on weather conditions.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} A typical flower has five petals yellow at opening that elongate into red, nectar-bearing spurs and alternate with five red, petal like sepals.{{sfn|Bare|1979|p=116}} However, flowers can have four or six petals and a matching number of sepals.{{sfn|Herlihy|Eckert|2007|p=1664}} Rarely, flowers in the wild can be entirely salmon, yellow,{{sfn|Gleason|Cronquist|1991|p=60}} or white.{{sfn|Nold|2003|p=73}} The flowers are nodding, hanging downwards with the spurs pointing up and the many [[stamen]]s projecting downwards together.{{sfn|Britton|Brown|1913|p=92}} The flowers are showy and measure {{Convert abbreviated|2 to 5|cm|4=1}} from the ends of the stamens to the tips of the spurs. Petals measure {{Convert abbreviated|2 to 3.6|cm|4=1}} from end of the spur to the outer edge.{{sfn|Sutherland|1986|p=89}}

The [[anther]]s on the stamens open to release their pollen before the [[Stigma (botany)|stigmas]] becomes receptive to aid cross pollination by visitors to the flowers.{{sfn|Bare|1979|p=116}} The flowers produce abundant dilute nectar,{{sfn|Griffin|Mavraganis|Eckert|2000|p=1247}} and attract hummingbirds, bumblebees, [[hawkmoth]]s, and other bees.{{sfn|Macior|1966|pp=302–304}} The [[ruby-throated hummingbird]] (''Archilochus colubris)'' is the primary pollinator.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}}

After pollination, Canadian columbines produce an upright cluster of five pod-shaped [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]] {{Convert abbreviated|1.5-3|cm|4=1}} long, which taper into a long, slender beak.{{sfn|Sutherland|1986|p=89}} When mature, the follicles split along one side to release numerous small shiny, black seeds, 1.5–2 millimeters by 0.5–1 mm.{{sfn|Bare|1979|p=116}} Seeds develop rapidly, reaching maturity around two weeks after flowering.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}}

Plants typically flower in their second year, and natural reseeding allows colonies to persist, despite individual plants having a short lifespan.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}}{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} Plants are shorter lived when growing in rich soils.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}}

== Taxonomy ==
[[File:Aquilegia canadensis WFNY-065.jpg|thumb|Illustration from ''Wild Flowers of New York'', 1918{{sfn|House|1918|p=Plate 65}}]]
''Aquilegia canadensis'' was given its binomial name by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. It is classified in the genus ''[[Aquilegia]]'' within the [[Ranunculaceae]] family. It has no accepted [[Variety (botany)|varieties]], but has 11 among its 26 [[heterotypic synonym]]s.{{sfn|POWO|2026}}

=== Names ===
The species name, ''canadensis'', is [[Botanical Latin]] meaning "belonging to Canada", a reference to where the first scientific specimens were gathered.{{sfn|Holloway|2005|p=14}} The [[common name]]s ''Canadian columbine'' or ''Canada columbine'' are often used for this species.{{sfn|Whittemore|2020}}{{sfn|Phillips2003|p=82}} It is known by the name ''common columbine'' for its abundance throughout much of its native range.{{sfn|Holloway|2005|p=14}} It is also called ''red columbine'',{{sfn|VASCAN 2026}} however this name is used for other species including ''[[Aquilegia elegantula]]''.{{sfn|Guennel|1995|p=259}} It is additionally known as ''eastern columbine'',{{sfn|Johnson|2001|p=104}} ''eastern red columbine'',{{sfn|Frey|LeBuhn|2016|p=204}} ''wild red columbine'',{{sfn|VASCAN 2026}} ''wild columbine'',{{sfn|Choukas-Bradley|2007|p=43}} ''American columbine'',{{sfn|VASCAN 2026}} and ''rock bells''.{{sfn|Edsall|1985|p=48}}

Among children the species was called ''honeysuckle'' because they would bite off the end of the spurs for the sweet nectar inside,{{sfn|Sanders|2003|p=33}} it was most often used in Illinois, Massachusetts, and Wisconsin alongside the name ''honey horns''.{{sfn|Coffey|1993|p=11}} Other regional names include ''meetinghouses'' from [[New England]], ''jacket-and-breeches'', ''Jack-in-trousers'', and ''lady's slipper'' in Massachusetts, ''red-bells'' and ''rock-lily'' from New Hampshire, and simply ''bells'' in Ohio. The names ''akeley'' and ''culverwort'' in English and {{lang|fr|ancolie}} or {{lang|fr|Gants de Notre-Dame}} in French are from Quebec while the name ''cluckies'' comes from Nova Scotia.{{sfn|Coffey|1993|p=11}} Like other species in the genus it is also simply called ''columbine''.{{sfn|Packard|Ross|1997|p=69}}

In the [[Omaha–Ponca language]] ''Aquilegia canadensis'' is called {{lang|oma|inubthoⁿ-kithe-sabe-hi}}, translating to "black perfume plant", related to one of its uses. In the [[Pawnee language]] it is known as {{lang|paw|skalikatit}} or as {{lang|paw|skarikatit}} meaning "black seed".{{sfn|Gilmore|1919|p=82}}

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Aquilegia canadensis'' is a native to [[Eastern North America|eastern]] and central North America, from [[New Brunswick]] to northern Florida and west to [[Saskatchewan]] and Texas.{{sfn|NRCS|2026b}} It is the sole native columbine from eastern North America,{{sfn|FS Staff|n.d.}} though [[smallflower columbine]] (''Aquilegia brevistyla'') is reported as far east as [[Clay County, Minnesota]] and northern parts of Ontario and the non-native [[European columbine]] (''Aquilegia vulgaris'') has escaped from cultivation in Canada, the northeast, and parts of the south.{{sfnm|1a1=NRCS|1y=2026a|2a1=NRCS|2y=2026c}}

In Canada it is native, but possibly [[locally extinct]], in the eastern province of New Brunswick.{{sfn|VASCAN 2026}} In Quebec it is found in the areas near the [[St. Lawrence River]],{{sfn|Marie-Victorin|Brouillet|Goulet|1995|p=228}} but not in the northern or eastern parts of the province.{{sfn|FS Staff|n.d.}} Similarly it is found throughout [[Southern Ontario]], but only in the southern half of [[Northern Ontario]] to the west.{{sfn|Dickinson et al. 2004|p=354}} It also grows in southern Manitoba, but only in the easternmost part of southern Saskatchewan.{{sfn|FS Staff|n.d.}}

In the [[Midwestern United States]] Canadian columbine is native to every state, but reaches its western limits in the Dakotas, Nebraska, Kansas, and Oklahoma. Its range extends almost to Wyoming in northern Nebraska, but is otherwise only in the easternmost portions of these states. Though native to Iowa, much of the central part of the state has no record of the species.{{sfn|NRCS|2026b}} In Missouri it is found throughout the state except for small areas of the southwest near Kansas and the southeastern lowlands.{{sfn|Steyermark|1996|p=678}} It is widespread in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Illinois as well as Indiana, Michigan, and Ohio.{{sfn|NRCS|2026b}}

In the [[Northeastern United States]] it is recorded in every state from Maine to New Jersey, with records of the species in every county of Pennsylvania. In the [[Southeastern United States]] it is native to every state except for Louisiana. However, it is only common in northern parts of the south such as Virginia, West Virginia, and Kentucky. It becomes much less widespread in North Carolina and Tennessee and is only known from a few counties in South Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama. It only grows in the Florida panhandle and is only found in [[Tishomingo County, Mississippi]]. Likewise it mostly grows in northern parts of Arkansas.{{sfn|NRCS|2026b}} The population in Texas is [[Disjunct distribution|disjunct]] from the rest of the range, growing only on the [[Edwards Plateau]].{{sfn|FS Staff|n.d.}}

''A. canadensis'' typically inhabits woodlands, forest edges, rocky slopes, and shaded bluffs.{{sfn|Wennerberg|2006|p=2}}{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} It will prefer well-drained, sandy or rocky soil, and will thrive in an area that experiences light to moderate shade. ''A. canadensis'' is best suited for sites that are not waterlogged or overly nutrient-rich.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}}{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} Due to its ability to both self and sexually reproduce, ''A. canadensis'' can maintain stable populations across a wide range of habitats.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}}

== Ecology ==

=== Reproduction ===
''Aquilegia canadensis'' has a mixed mating system, where they are able to both self-pollinate and outcross. The species is fully self-compatible, and has the ability to produce seeds without a pollinator.{{sfn|Eckert|Schaefer|1998|p=921}} However, despite being self-compatible, it does not fully compensate for the absence of pollinators, since fruit and seed production is lowered when pollinators are not present.{{sfn|Eckert|Schaefer|1998|p=922}}

One major factor that influences the selfing and outcrossing balance is the herkogamy of the anther and stigma. There is genetic variation in the separation of the reproductive structures between different populations, and plants that have greater separation between the anther and stigma have lower rates of autonomous selfing and are more prone to outcrossing.{{sfn|Herlihy|Eckert|2007|p=1670}} The separation is primarily due to differences in the pistil length, rather than positioning of the structures. The genetic difference in herkogamy between populations suggests that it can evolve through selection to regulate mating strategies.{{sfn|Herlihy|Eckert|2007|p=1670}}

Pollination is primarily carried out through the Ruby-Throated Hummingbird (''Archilochus colubris),'' which is able to access the nectar stored in the elongated spurs of the flower.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} The Canadian columbine is one of the eight most important nectar sources for hummingbirds in eastern North America.{{sfn|Proctor|Yeo|Lack|1996|p=229}} In addition, bumblebees, hawk moths, and other bees also contribute to outcrossing between flowers.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}}{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} Genetic studies between ''A. canadensis'' and its sister species, ''A. brevistyla'', which is primarily bee-pollinated, have shown that the shift to hummingbird pollination is associated with changes to spur curvature, floral pigmentation, and nectar traits.{{sfn|Edwards et al. 2021|pp=2212–2213}}

Reproductive success is also reliant on the size of the population. Plants that grow in larger and more densely populated sites produce significantly more fruits and seeds per plant, in comparison to plants in smaller populations.{{sfn|Mavraganis|Eckert|2001|pp=305–306}} Spatial isolation by itself does not have a large effect on reproductive output, but smaller population sizes reduces the opportunities for pollinator visits and outcrossing.{{sfn|Mavraganis|Eckert|2001|p=307–308}}

The [[rusty patched bumblebee]] (''Bombus affinis'') has been documented cutting holes in the spurs to engage in [[nectar robbing]].{{sfn|Holm|2014|p=143}} Both queens and workers of the rusty patched bumblebee cut holes in the spurs, with some queens collecting pollen before cutting holes to take nectar. Workers either collected pollen or engaged in nectar robbing, not both behaviors at the same flower. Workers and queens both sometimes acquired nectar at the mouth of the flower rather than nectar robbing.{{sfn|Macior|1966|p=304}} Though other species have not been recorded making holes in the nectar spurs,{{sfn|Holm|2014|p=143}} the [[golden northern bumble bee]] (''Bombus fervidus'') do sometimes make use of holes that have already been made as well as collecting nectar from the mouth of the flower.{{sfn|Macior|1968|p=1033}} Both [[honeybee]]s and ''[[Lasioglossum]]'' sweat bees also use previously created perforations.{{sfn|Macior|1966|p=304}} Many other species of bumblebee collect nectar from Canadian columbine including the [[two-spotted bumble bee]], [[brown-belted bumblebee]], [[common eastern bumblebee]], [[Nevada bumblebee]], and [[American bumblebee]]. The [[half-black bumblebee]] both collects nectar and pollen from the flowers.{{sfn|Macior|1968|p=1034}}

=== Disease and herbivory ===
[[File:Effect of leaf miners on Aquilegia canadensis (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|alt=Photograph of leaf miner damage on an Aquilegia canadensis leaf|Leaf miner damage to an ''A. canadensis'' leaf]]
''Aquilegia canadensis'' does not generally experience high rates of disease or herbivory in its native range. The most common issue is caused by leaf miner activity, as they create serpentine trail in the leaves, but is not major problem with the damage caused is generally only cosmetic.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} It is a host plant for the [[columbine duskywing]] butterfly (''Erynnis lucilius'') and the [[columbine borer]] moth (''Papaipema leucostigma'').{{sfn|Holm|2014|p=143}} It is also fed upon by the non-native columbine sawfly (''[[Pristiphora rufipes]]''),{{sfn|Prous et al. 2017|pp=107–108}} which can rapidly reduce leaves to just their veins.{{sfn|Holm|2014|p=143}} However, ''A. canadensis'' is resistant to deer and rabbit browsing.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} ''A. canadensis'' has a chemical defense system. When plant tissues are damaged it releases hydrogen cyanide (HCN).{{sfn|Alfs|2001|pp=99–100}}

==Cultivation==
''Aquilegia canadensis'' is a highly decorative plant, valued for its attractive foliage and showy flowers. For this reason it is widely grown outside its native region, in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere.

The plant grows best in light to moderate shade, and prefers well-drained sandy loams, thriving in limestone-based or circumneutral soils.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}}{{sfn|Wennerberg|2006|p=2}}{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} Plants grown in soils that are too moist or rich may produce weak plants, and have a shorter lifespan.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} Despite being a short-lived perennial, it self seeds very readily, allowing it to persist for many years.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}} Seedlings generally flower in their second year. Cool-moist stratification at {{Cvt|5|C|F}} for three to four weeks may speed sprouting, but it is not required for germination.{{sfn|Wennerberg|2006|p=2}} Mature plants are able to tolerate periods of drought, but growth is best under consistent moisture.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}} Seeds can be stored for three to four months in seedbags at {{Cvt|5|to(-)|6|C|F}}.{{sfn|Wennerberg|2006|p=2}}

Several [[cultivar]]s are commonly grown, including 'Corbett', a dwarf form with yellow flowers; 'Nana', which only produces all-yellow flowers; and 'Pink Lanterns', which has pink and white blossoms.{{sfn|Wennerberg|2006|p=2}}{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}}

== In culture ==
''Aquilegia canadensis'' has been used in several cultures across North America. In several Native American communities, seeds are crushed and rubbed on the hands to act as a love charm.{{sfn|LBJWC Staff|2023}} The species is cultivated in gardens for its ornamental value, as its flowers and ability to thrive in shade have made it a popular feature in gardens. Several cultivars are commonly grown for their features, including their distinct flower color and size.{{sfn|Mahr|n.d.}}

A traditional use by the [[Omaha people|Omaha]] and [[Ponca]] is to produce a perfume. The black seeds of the plant are gathered and crushed, often being chewed by the Omaha. The resulting paste would be spread on items of clothing and the fragrance would retained for a long time, often being more noticeable when clothing became damp with rain or dew. In the traditions of [[Pawnee people]] the seed is used to produce a perfume that is also reputed to act as a love charm. In Pawnee [[traditional medicine]] it is a reputed cure for fever or headache if the seeds were crushed to powder in a mortar and pestle made of elm-wood and then made into a drink in hot water.{{sfn|Gilmore|1919|p=82}} In the traditional medicine of the [[Cherokee]] a tea is made from Canadian columbine for "heart trouble".{{sfn|Hamel|Chiltoskey|1975|p=30}}
